title: City-paid meal providers in the food-safety inspection files
question: Do organisations the City pays for meals and food have poor food-safety inspection results while being paid?
finding: 48 City-paid food vendors were found in the health department's inspection files on two keys (name and their own address), 185 facilities in all. Of the 23 paid at least $250,000 under meal or food programme contracts ($300.1 million, fiscal 2019 to 2027), 3 of 55 facilities (5.5%) ever had a closure, conditional pass or score under 71, against 13.1% of all 13,625 inspected facilities. Two programme kitchens were closed: the Salvation Army's 407 9th Street kitchen (15 and 16 May 2024) and Centro Latino's 1656 15th Street senior meal site (12 January 2023).
how: Vendors: every payee in the Controller's vouchers with the Food sub-object or a meal, food, nutrition, catering or grocery word in the contract title, $25,000 or more. A vendor's own addresses come from its City business registration (owner or trade name) and its IRS exempt-organisation record (by name, or by the tax number the project matched earlier). A facility counts only when its address is one of those AND its name shares the vendor's distinctive name words. Inspection results: 2016-2019 scores (under 71 is the department's 'poor' band); 2020 onward pass, conditional pass or closure. 'Meal programme' = paid $250,000 or more under contract titles naming meals, nutrition, congregate, home-delivered, food or groceries.
limits: An inspection is of a kitchen permit, not of a contract; the files do not say where the City's meals were cooked, and a vendor may cook at a site under another name. Closures are often lifted within days once a fault is fixed (Centro Latino's was corrected the same day). Address matching misses vendors registered at an office address and kitchens outside the City (Moonstar Buffet has no facility in the files). The files have gaps (see the next screen). Small caterers paid for meeting food appear here with ordinary restaurant results.
